.and the feedback $u = Fx$ is chosen so that $A + B_2F$ is stable and
$$
J_0 = \|Tx_w\|_2^2
$$
is minimized. For simplicity, we shall assume that $D_{12}^*D_{12} = I$ and $D_{12}^*C_1 = 0$. It is routine to verify that $J_0 = \mathrm{Trace}(B_1B_1^*X)$ where $X = X^* \ge 0$ satisfies
$$
T(X,F) := X(A+B_2F)+(A+B_2F)^*X+(C_1+D_{12}F)^*(C_1+D_{12}F) = 0.
$$
Hence the optimal control problem becomes a constrained minimization problem, and we can use the Lagrange multipliers method outlined above. (Note that in this case, the variable $x$ takes the form $x = \left[ \begin{array}{l} \mathrm{Vec}X \\ \mathrm{Vec}F \end{array} \right]$). Let
$$
J(X,F) := J_0 + \mathrm{Trace}(T(X,F)P)
$$
with $P = P^*$. We first verify the regularity conditions: the equation
$$
\nabla \mathrm{Trace}(T(X,F)P) = 0
$$
or, equivalently,
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial \mathrm{Trace}(T(X,F)P)}{\partial X} \\
\frac{\partial \mathrm{Trace}(T(X,F)P)}{\partial F}
\end{bmatrix}
= \left[ \begin{array}{c}
P(A+B_2F)^*+(A+B_2F)P \\
2(B_2^*X+F)P
\end{array} \right] = 0
$$
has a unique solution $P = 0$ since $A + B_2F$ is assumed to be stable at the minimum point. Hence regularity conditions are satisfied. Now the necessary condition for local optimum can be applied:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial J(X,F)}{\partial X} &= B_1B_1^* + P(A + B_2F)^* + (A + B_2F)P = 0 \\
\frac{\partial J(X,F)}{\partial F} &= 2(B_2^*X + F)P = 0 \\
\frac{\partial J(X,F)}{\partial P} &= X(A + B_2F) + (A + B_2F)^*X + (C_1 + D_{12}F)^*(C_1 + D_{12}F) = 0. \quad (20.4)
\end{aligned}
$$
It should be pointed out that, in general, we cannot conclude from equation (20.3) that $B_2^*X + F = 0$. Care must be exercised to arrive at such a conclusion. For example, if we assume that $B_1$ is square and nonsingular, then we know that if $F$ is such that $A + B_2F$ is stable, then $P > 0$. Hence we have
$$
F = -B_2^*X,
$$
and we substitute this relation into equation (20.4) and get the familiar Riccati equation:
$$
XA + A^*X - XB_2B_2^*X + C_1^*C_1 = 0.
$$
This Riccati equation has a stabilizing solution if $(A, B_2)$ is stabilizable and if $(C_1, A)$ has no unobservable modes on the imaginary axis. Indeed, in this case, the controller thus obtained is a global optimal control law.

.In this section, we shall use the Lagrange multiplier method to derive some necessary conditions for a fixed-order controller that minimizes an $ \mathcal{H}_{2} $ performance. We shall again consider a standard system setup.

where the system $ G $ is $ n $-th order with a realization given by

$$ G(s) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{A}{C_{1}} & \frac{B_{1}}{D_{12}} \\ \frac{B_{2}}{C_{1}} & \frac{0}{D_{12}} \end{bmatrix}. $$

For simplicity, we shall assume that

(i) $(A, B_{1})$ is stableizable and $(C_{1}, A)$ is detectable;

(ii) $(A, B_{2})$ is stableizable and $(C_{2}, A)$ is detectable;

(iii) $D_{12}^{*} = \begin{bmatrix} C_{1} & D_{12} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & I \end{bmatrix}$;

(iv) $\begin{bmatrix} B_{1} \\ D_{21} \end{bmatrix} D_{21}^{*} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ I \end{bmatrix}.

We shall be interested in the following fixed order $ \mathcal{H}_{2} $ optimal controller problem: given an integer $ n_{c} \leq n $, find an $ n_{c} $-th order controller

$ K = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{A_{c}}{C_{c}} & \frac{B_{c}}{D_{12}} \end{bmatrix} $

that internally stabilizes the system $ G $ and minimizes the $ \mathcal{H}_{2} $ norm of the transfer matrix $ T_{z_{w}} $. For technical reasons, we will further assume that the realization of the controller is minimal, i.e., $(A_{c}, B_{c})$ is controllable and $(C_{c}, A_{c})$ is observable.

Suppose a such controller exists, and then the closed loop transfer matrix $ T_{z_{w}} $ can be written as

$ T_{z_{w}} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{A}{B_{c}C_{2}} & B_{2}C_{c} \\ \frac{B_{2}}{C_{1}} & D_{12}C_{c} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\tilde{A}}{C} & \frac{\tilde{B}}{0} \end{bmatrix} $.

### Section1.4 Matrix Factorizations

#### 21.4.1 Inner Functions

A transfer matrix \(N(z)\) is called **inner** if \(N(z)\) is stable and \(N^*(z)N(z) = I\) for all \(z = e^{j\theta}\). Note that if \(N\) has no poles at the origin, then \(N^*(e^{j\theta}) = N^-(e^{j\theta})\). A transfer matrix is called **outer** if all its transmission zeros are stable (i.e., inside of the unit disc).

**Lemma 21.14** Let \(N = \begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{bmatrix}\) and suppose that \(X = X^*\) satisfies

\[\begin{aligned}
& A^*XA - X + C^*C = 0.
\end{aligned}\]

Then

(a) \(D^*C + B^*XA = 0\) implies \(N^*N = (D - CA^{-1}B)^*D\);
(b) \(X \ge 0\), \((A,B)\) controllable, and \(N^*N = (D - CA^{-1}B)^*D\) implies \(D^*C + B^*XA = 0\).

**Proof.** The results follow by noting the following equality:

\[\begin{aligned}
& N^-(z)N(z) = \begin{bmatrix} A & 0 & B \\ (A^*)^{-1}C^*C & (A^*)^{-1} & (A^*)^{-1}C^*D \\ (D - CA^{-1}B)^*C & -B^*(A^*)^{-1} & (D - CA^{-1}B)^*D \end{bmatrix} \\
& \quad = \begin{bmatrix} A & 0 & B \\ 0 & (A^*)^{-1} & XB + (A^*)^{-1}C^*D \\ D^*C + B^*XA & -B^*(A^*)^{-1} & (D - CA^{-1}B)^*D \end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}\]

The following corollary is a special case of this lemma which gives the necessary and sufficient conditions of a discrete inner transfer matrix with the state-space representation.

**Corollary 21.15** Suppose that \(N(z) = \begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{bmatrix} \in \mathcal{HR}_\infty\) is a controllable realization; then \(N(z)\) is inner if and only if there exists a matrix \(X = X^* \ge 0\) such that

(a) \(A^*XA - X + C^*C = 0\)
(b) \(D^*C + B^*XA = 0\)
(c) \((D - CA^{-1}B)^*D = D^*D + B^*XB = I\).

21.4.2 Coprime Factorizations

Recall that two transfer matrices $M(z), N(z) \in \mathcal{R H}_\infty$ are said to be right coprime if $\begin{bmatrix} M & \\ N \end{bmatrix}$ is left invertible in $\mathcal{R}H_\infty$ i.e., $\exists U, V \in \mathcal{R}H_\infty$ such that

$$U(z)N(z) + V(z)M(z) = I.$$

The left coprime is defined analogously. A plant $G(z) \in \mathcal{R}L_\infty$ is said to have double coprime factorization if $\exists$ a right coprime factorization $G = NM^{-1}$, a left coprime factorization $G = \tilde{M}^{-1}\tilde{N}$, and $U, V, \tilde{U}, \tilde{V} \in \mathcal{R}H_\infty$ such that

$$\begin{bmatrix} V & U \\ -\tilde{N} & \tilde{M} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} M & -\tilde{U} \\ N & \tilde{V} \end{bmatrix} = I. \tag{21.23}$$

The stated space formulae for discrete time transfer matrix coprime factorization are the same as for the continuous time. They are given by the following theorem.

Theorem 21.18 Let $G(z) = \begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{bmatrix} \in \mathcal{R}L_\infty$ be a stabilizable and detectable realization. Choose $F$ and $L$ such that $A + BF$ and $A + LC$ are both stable. Let $U, V, \tilde{U}, \tilde{V}, N, M, \tilde{N},$ and $\tilde{M}$ be given as follows

$$\begin{bmatrix} M & \\ N \end{bmatrix} \coloneqq \begin{bmatrix} A + BF & BZ_r \\ F & Z_r \\ C + DF & DZ_r \end{bmatrix}$$

$$\begin{bmatrix} \tilde{U} & \\ \tilde{V} \end{bmatrix} \coloneqq \begin{bmatrix} A + BF & LZ_l^{-1} \\ F & 0 \\ -(C + DF) & Z_l^{-1} \end{bmatrix}$$

$$\begin{bmatrix} \tilde{M} & \\ \tilde{N} \end{bmatrix} \coloneqq \begin{bmatrix} A + LC & L & B + LD \\ Z_lC & Z_l & Z_lD \end{bmatrix}$$

$$\begin{bmatrix} U & \\ V \end{bmatrix} \coloneqq \begin{bmatrix} A + LC & L & -(B + LD) \\ Z_l^{-1}F & 0 & Z_l^{-1} \end{bmatrix}$$

where $Z_r$ and $Z_l$ are any nonsingular matrices. Then $G = NM^{-1} = \tilde{M}^{-1}\tilde{N}$ are rcf and lcf, respectively, and (21.23) is satisfied.

### Page 185

ractive matter.## 2. STATEMENT OF THE MAIN THEOREM:

Theorem 21.20 states that the transformation of the covariance matrix of a Rayleigh distribution \( G(z) \) to a new variable \( B \) is given by:
\[ B = A + BF = AR^{-1/2} \]

This implies:
\[ R^2 = \frac{A+B+A+B^2}{AA} = \frac{A+B+A+B}{AA} = \frac{1+A+B+A+B^2-A}{AA} = 1 + (B - A) = 1 + R - A \]
which is the Pearson's equation for Rayleigh distribution.

Theorems 21.21 and 21.22 extend to the case of normal distributions:

Theorem 21.21: Let a normal distribution \( G \) have the Matern class \( M \) covariance matrix \( A \). Then the relationship between \( z \) and \( B \) is given by:

\[ B = \frac{AR^{-1/2} + A + BF}{A + BF} \]

where \( R \) is the Matern class \( M \) radius of gyration, and \( A \) and \( F \) are the mean and covariance of the normal distribution \( G \), respectively.

Theorem 21.22: For a normal distribution \( G \) with parameters \( A \) and \( M \),

- \( A \) is the scale of the distribution.
- \( M \) is the Matern class of the distribution.
- The sum of \( M \) and \( F \) must be less than or equal to \( M \). However, since \( M \) is the Matern class of the distribution, \( M \geq 1 \).

Given these definitions, we can state that the relationship between a normal distribution and a transformed variable \( B \) follows:

\[ B = A + BF = AR^{-1/2} + A + BF = AR^{-1/2} + A + BF = AR^{-1/2} + A + BF \]

This equation represents the relationship between a normal distribution and its transformed variable, indicating how the distribution parameter and \( B \) coordinate are related.

h) Step 8. Error analysis. The errors in the finite element method are first analyzed in general terms by re-expressing the present examples in terms of the previously defined model. The results are found to be very good for each specific case. It is then demonstrated that this method is numerically stable and that there are not any errors due to numerical instability. As we shall see, the errors introduced to the vibration analysis go beyond the numerical error due to the identical mesh structure. This numerical error is rapidly increased by a factor \(1/\Delta x\) or \(1/\sqrt{2}\), and care needs to be taken to convert the actual error \(1/\Delta \Psi\). Hopefully, this work shows that this error in vibration analysis will not influence those numerical results obtained by using the modal correction method.

In an analysis of a nonlinear system, it is important to obtain a solution which is not disturbed in time. This is because many physical variables within the system change in time. In the following example, we demonstrate the use of the Ritz theory to solve the general case. The left panel of Fig. 1 shows the change in the mean disease prevalence by the grid size during every weekend with a kernel size of zero. The model has been run for thirty-week cycles. The right panel shows the standard deviation of the defeat by a grid size of one as compared with the grid size of one starting from at different calculation points. (Rice et al., 1998) As can be seen, a dramatic shift towards the whole system level is observed when the grid size is increased by 100%. Above 100% the distribution of the defeatatio by a grid size of 70% to 100% is the same for all grid sizes and (Bollte et al., 2005) the distribution of the total population weight is already similar to the distribution of the defeatatio by the same the size. The right panel also shows that the difference is greater the smaller the grid size, which is reflected in the equation of the right panel. (Ailer & Pande, 2000) The right panel at a close distance shows that the case the effect of the resistance parameter by a start of the epidemic (Fig. 2 and 3) is larger the smaller the grid size.
